statement: A point starts at (1, 2). It is reflected in the line x = 3, then in the line x = 7, then in x = 3 again, then in x = 7 again, and so on, taking turns. Where is the point after 10 reflections?

choices.misconception: I thought each pair of reflections moves the point by the distance between the lines, 4, instead of twice that distance.
I thought every single reflection moves the point 8 to the right, so I added 80.
I thought reflecting twice always brings a point back to where it started, so 10 reflections change nothing.
I found that each pair of reflections moves the point 8 units, but I moved it to the left instead of the right.

hints: Work out the first two reflections carefully. Where does the point end up?
Reflecting in two parallel lines one after the other is the same as a slide. Find how far and which way one pair of reflections moves the point, then use that five times.
After two reflections the point is at (9, 2): it has moved 8 to the right.

solutions.reliable: Reflecting (1, 2) in x = 3 gives (5, 2), since 1 is 2 to the left of the line and 5 is 2 to the right of it. Reflecting (5, 2) in x = 7 gives (9, 2). So one pair of reflections moves the point 8 to the right. The 10 reflections are 5 such pairs, so the point moves $5 \times 8 = 40$ to the right and ends at (41, 2). Checking the next pair: (9, 2) goes to (-3, 2) and then to (17, 2), again 8 further right. The transferable idea: two reflections in parallel lines make a slide of twice the distance between the lines.

whyOnTest: Tests composing transformations: two reflections in parallel lines combine into a slide of twice the gap, not a return to the start.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
